newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest seen cool this week, then hot and dry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest seen cool this week, then hot and dry.

text.p: A cold front should bring normal to below normal temperatures to the U.S. Midwest this week but meteorologists said another hot, dry spell would hit the Corn Belt by Friday.

"We're going to get back into some very pleasant days with highs in the upper 70s (degrees Fahrenheit) to lower 80s," said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. "By the weekend, we'll be looking at temperatures close to what we had this weekend."
Temperatures this past weekend topped 95 degrees F from Nebraska to Indiana.
The heat wave broke late Sunday as a front pushed through but forecasters said rainfall amounts were less than expected in central and southern Illinois and Indiana.
"The rains came into western Illinois and just died," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster with Weather Express Inc.
Gesser said rainfall amounts totalled 0.10 to 0.50 inch with 10 to 20 percent coverage across dry pockets of central and southern Illinois.
Showers were moving toward the Ohio Valley on Monday, bringing a chance for thunderstorms.
Meteorologists said long-range forecasts suggested temperatures would heat up again by Friday with only light showers expected in central and southern Illinois.

"The ability to drive those showers south does not look very promising," Palmerino said. "Once you get into southern Iowa, Missouri and most of Illinois, you're probably looking at no more than 0.10 to 0.50 inch with less than 50 percent coverage."
Temperatures were expected to remain in the 90s F through early next week, Palmerino and Gesser said.
Hot, dry weather during pollination can stress the corn crop.
"The heat may persist," Palmerino said. "This one doesn't look like the heat will break all that quickly. Above normal temperatures may continue into early next week."
Gesser said a few showers may reach the northern Corn Belt next week but would likely miss central Illinois. He put coverage at 30 to 40 percent from August 2 through 4.

"The next cold front appears to be sort of a dud for the Corn Belt," Gesser said. "Right now I'm not putting much rain south of a line from Chicago to Toledo. It looks like we're looking at six days of low to upper 90s for the Corn Belt with no significant rains.
"Right now both the European and the American model are bringing the heat back and are not suggesting any rains."
